awd_titl_txt: Conference: Regional Applied Interdisciplinary Numerical (Cascade RAIN) conference in the Cascade Mountains area
awd_abstract_narration:
The "Regional Applied Interdisciplinary Numerical (Cascade RAIN) in the Cascade Mountains area" conference will convene on the Oregon State campus on April 26, 2025. The conference will bring together faculty and students from across the Pacific Northwest to facilitate the exchange of scientific advancements in the area of computational mathematics and interdisciplinary applications. Presentations are expected to cover almost all topics within computational mathematics including state-of-the-art methods for numerical partial differential equations and foundational mathematics of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Through the use of travel support, the conference will seek to broaden the participation across this geographic area and reach the broadest possible cohort including graduate students and junior faculty in the region. The conference will also feature mini-tutorials on basic and advanced computational mathematics and the mathematics of data science as a means of engaging both less prepared and more senior participants in research in computational mathematics. Furthermore, this conference will seek to foster future collaborative efforts between participants at all career stages.  

This conference will provide support for the participants of the conference and aims to bring together researchers across many career stages including senior, junior faculty and other researchers as well as students involved in computational mathematics across its different aspects including numerical analysis and interdisciplinary work. The participants will gain new insights and perspectives in computational mathematics and various application domains from researchers in local universities. The specific minitutorials include hands-on training of advanced finite-difference and finite-volume methods for initial boundary value problems as well as unsupervised and supervised learning methods. The website of the conference is https://sites.google.com/oregonstate.edu/rain2025

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Intellectual Merit:

 

The Cascade RAIN ’25 conference took place on Saturday, April 26, 2025 in Corvallis, OR at Oregon State University campus. There were two additional days: Friday, April 25, 2025 and Sunday, April 27, 2025 devoted to the mini tutorials which served as satellite events. 

The conference provided in-person opportunities for research 

dissemination and exchange of recent advances in computational mathematics and mathematics of data science in the Cascade Mountains area. 

 

The conference was advertised with a call for participation from Fall 2024 to early April 2025, and a website  https://sites.google.com/oregonstate.edu/rain2025 was used as a primary tool for dissemination and registration.  

 

A Local Organizing Committee of Nathan Gibson,  Jane Shaw MacDonald, Nicholas Marshall, Malgorzata Peszynska, Ralph Showalter was formed; these were four OSU faculty plus one postdoc (MacDonald).  This Committee also constituted the travel support committee.  

 

There was also a group of local graduate students hailing from the OSU SIAM student chapter who helped and supported the organizational efforts. Some of these students also served as mentors for the Minitutorial I (Tyler Fara, Praveenin Mathangadeera, Madison Phelps) and Minitutorial II (Peter Cowal, Wyatt Whiting). Other students involved in organizational support for the conference included Azar Asgari, Stefanie Fazekas, Nicholas Harrison, Bailey Sharon. 

 

The meeting enabled extensive discussions and opened doors for potential local collaborations for cohorts of researchers; we achieved the goals of engaging a broad and varied group of researchers from the area. Over 95 participants registered interest and in the end 66 attended including 47  graduate students, 4 undergraduate students, 5 early career researchers and 10  other faculty.  These participants were from Boise State, Lane CC, Portland State, University of Oregon, University of Washington, Washington State University (Vancouver and Pullman campuses), and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in addition to Oregon State University. 

 

The meeting featured 33 talks. The talks were 10 min long, and the schedule was established in a random fashion in the informal style reminiscent of the Finite Element circus. Of these, 25 talks were given by the graduate students. The subject of talks ranged from numerical PDEs and applications, through mathematical biology to data science. 

 

The minitutorials were attended by 16 participants and were conducted in a classroom with laptop use at Oregon State University; there were downloadable materials including slides and code provided by the organizers; the tutorials provided hands-on activities. Minitutorial I  (Friday, April 25, 2025, prepared by M. Peszynska)  on  "Introduction to Computational  Modeling" covered intermediate and advanced topics on (i) Transition to the programming in compilable environments, (ii) Modeling phenomena with complex data and  (iii) Modeling with selected transient nonlinear differential equations, had 11 participants.  Minitutorial II (Sunday, April 27, 2025, prepared by N. Marshall) on "Mathematics of Unsupervised Learning Methods" had 11 participants.  The minitutorials engaged additional three (Friday) and two (Thursday) advanced graduate students from OSU Mathematics who helped to prepare and test the materials and mentored the participants in their projects.    

 

Broader Impacts: 

 

The CASCADE 2025 conference support provided by this project helped the participants of the talks, as well as minitutorial participants, to obtain, augment, and refine their research skills in computational mathematics and mathematics of data science.

 

The Cascade RAIN ’25 conference funds provided support for the travel of early-career researchers and graduate students. In particular, travel support was allotted to 11 participants from Boise State University, University Washington, University of Illinois Springfield, Portland State University,Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Washington State University (Vancouver and Pullman) . The funds were also used to support local subsistence expenses of others, and were complemented by the Mathematics department support. 

Due to the considerable delay in certainty of getting the funds, some participants were not able to attend the conference, even though more than 97 registered.  In the end,  there were some left over funds unused for travel support which will be returned to the NSF.  

 

The minitutorials as well as the efforts of the local student helpers supporting the organizing committee provided an additional professional development opportunity for 9 graduate students and one early career faculty involved who helped to mentor and coordinate the event's organization.
